sentences.text: What is a monitor's secrecy worth?
AI monitors often work from written rules, and agents share workspaces.
In one security evaluation this year, about 1,200 agents found a shared cache and turned it into a message board.
So if one agent can read the monitor's rules, does that knowledge spread to a saboteur?
And how much does it help?
We built a two-agent test.
Two language-model agents share one job: place 12 records and tag each with its destination.
A few records are restricted and must never reach the exit.
One agent may secretly be a saboteur.
After each game, a monitor reads the log and the chat and says flag or clean.
Its checklist has a documented gap: it reads a record's tag only at the moment the record moves to the exit.
A secured store in the workspace holds either that checklist or an unrelated note, and we vary who holds the key.
First, the pre-registered comparison.
Undetected sabotage was 0 of 50 without the checklist, and 0 of 54 when the honest agent held it.
But no honest keyholder ever opened the store, so the secret never moved.
When the saboteur held the key, 5 of 6 opened it and laundered a record's tag, exactly the move the gap allows.
The monitor still flagged all 6.
To measure what the rules are worth to an attacker, we scripted a library of attacks on fresh layouts and replayed every monitor on the same games.
Here, the saboteur posts a cover message, changes a restricted record's tag to the exit's own tag, and moves it out.
Both checklist monitors call it clean.
The same models without the checklist, or with the end state in view, flag it.
Across the library, knowing the checklist paid only against monitors whose decisions obey it.
With the checklist, gpt-oss-20b missed 75 of 100 rule-informed attacks and none of 50 naive ones.
Without the checklist, it missed 1.
Sonnet's checklist verdict missed 28 of 50, yet its own suspicion score separated every one of them from the honest games.
And one line explains those misses: change the checklist's last rule from "otherwise mark the run clean" to "use your own judgement", and Sonnet missed none.
And when a teammate simply asks for the store's contents?
The open-weight keyholder opened it in 35 of 60 games, but never repeated the checklist's wording.
Claude Haiku, the study's honest agent, kept it closed in all 60.
So, secrecy protects only monitors that obey their rules.
Don't end a monitor's checklist with "mark everything else clean", use calibrated scores where they separate attacks from honest runs, and check the end state when you can.
Our limits: one fictional task with two agents, hand-written attacks, and two-agent counts that stay provisional until the final results.
The code, the data and a replay viewer are open, and the open-weight results rerun offline.
